Bug: when adding projects in created them with windows admin and I had to retake them to fix it

What the spec step said it changed, its final output:

I couldn't find the cause in the spec. It said nothing about who owns the files Suspense creates, so I added a rule that everything it creates belongs to the signed-in user. `piton check` reports no problems, `piton build` wrote 79 files, and the new text is in the refreshed reference.

**The two likely causes:**
- **Suspense running as administrator.** Files an elevated process creates on Windows end up owned by the Administrators group.
- **Files written from the Podman machine.** A container run writes into the Windows project folder from inside a virtual machine, which can leave odd ownership.

The spec now rules out both, but the code step should confirm which one actually happened to you.

## What changed in the spec

**1. New "File Ownership" section** (`.claude/reference/scope/application/index.md#file-ownership`)
- **Who owns what:** every file and folder Suspense creates belongs to the user, as if you'd made it yourself, on every platform. That covers new project folders and their contents, `.suspense` data, files written by tasks or the editor, and Suspense's own files such as preferences.
- **No elevation on Windows:** Suspense declares that it runs with the rights of whoever starts it and never requires elevation. Its installer and self-update must not start it elevated either.
- **If it runs elevated anyway:** each file and folder it creates is still owned by the signed-in user, not Administrators, and takes its permissions from the folder it's in. The same applies to the programs it starts, including git's repository, so git never refuses a project as owned by someone else.
- **Never left behind:** nothing is ever left owned by Administrators, SYSTEM or another account.

**2. New Project** (`.claude/reference/scope/new-project/index.md#creating`): everything the form creates, Git repository included, belongs to you, so the project can be edited, built and committed right away with no ownership to take.

**3. Containers** (`.claude/reference/scope/container-environment/index.md#description`): on macOS and Windows, container runs act as you rather than root inside the Podman machine. Files they write into a folder mounted from Windows are yours and inherit that folder's permissions.

The constraints are in `.suspense/history/1791132843-ProjectsCreatedWithWindowsAdmin.understanding.md`.

## Anchors the code should follow
- `ApplicationScope`: `#file-ownership`. This covers the Windows build's setting that it runs without elevation, the installer, self-update, and setting ownership when Suspense finds itself elevated.
- `NewProjectScope`: `#creating`.
- `ContainerEnvironmentScope`: `#description`, for the user Podman runs containers as on Windows and macOS.

lines: +    // Run elevated all the same, what it and the programs it starts create
+//! Who owns what Suspense creates: the user running it, as though they had
+//! made it themselves, as the ApplicationScope's file ownership says.
+//! On Linux and macOS a process creates what it creates as its own user, and
+//! so nothing is needed there. Windows' build declares it runs as invoker,
+//! never asking for elevation (gpui's embedded manifest does so). Should it be
+//! started elevated all the same, as from an administrator's terminal, what an
+//! elevated process creates is owned by the Administrators group: the token's
+//! default owner is. So the process's token is made to give the signed-in
+//! user as the owner instead, before anything is created. Every program it
+//! starts, git and the harness among them, is given a copy of that token, so
+//! what they create is the user's too, and each file still takes the
+//! permissions it inherits from its folder.
+/// Makes the user the owner of everything this process, and every program it
+/// starts, creates from now on, where it was started elevated on Windows;
+        eprintln!("couldn't make the user the owner of what Suspense creates: {err}");
+        TOKEN_OWNER, TOKEN_QUERY, TOKEN_USER, TokenElevation, TokenOwner, TokenUser,
+    /// The process's token, closed when dropped.
+        let failed = |what: &str| format!("{what} failed ({})", unsafe { GetLastError() });
+        // Not elevated, what it creates is already the user's.
+        // The signed-in user, as the token names them.

content.text:
I've made two fixes, one for each likely cause, but I can't tell from here which one created your Administrators-owned projects. The Linux tests pass (512). I haven't been able to run anything on Windows, and the change to containers on macOS and Windows hasn't been tried against a real Podman machine.

**1. Suspense started elevated, such as from an administrator terminal.**
- **The cause:** on Windows, anything an elevated program creates is owned by the Administrators group.
- **The fix (`src/ownership.rs`):** at startup, if Suspense is running elevated, it changes its own access token so the signed-in user is the owner of everything it creates. Every program it starts gets a copy of that token, so git's repository and whatever the harness writes are yours too. Files still take their permissions from the folder they're in. Nothing changes when it isn't elevated, or on Linux and macOS.
- **Checked:** the full app can't be compiled for Windows on this machine (a C dependency needs a compiler that isn't installed). So I type-checked this module on its own for the Windows target, and it had no errors or warnings.

**2. Container runs on Windows and macOS.**
- **The cause:** on those platforms, runs used to act as root inside the Podman machine. Only Linux ran them as you.
- **The fix (`src/container.rs`):** every platform now passes `--userns=keep-id`, so a run acts as you, as the container spec now says. I added a test for this.
- **Risk:** some older Podman versions reject `--userns=keep-id` on a rootful machine. If container runs start failing on Windows or macOS, that's the first thing to check.

**Already in place, no change needed:**
- **No admin prompt:** the Windows build already declares that it runs with the rights of whoever starts it and never asks for elevation. A library it uses embeds that setting by default.
- **Self-update:** it relaunches `suspense.exe` as an ordinary program. It renames the download to `suspense.exe` first, so Windows' habit of elevating programs with "update" in their name doesn't kick in.
- **Installer:** there isn't one. Releases are a zip.

**To find out which cause hit you:** you'd have to have started Suspense from an administrator terminal or with "Run as administrator" for the first one. If you didn't, the container runs are the more likely cause.

**One edge case the code doesn't cover:** if Suspense is started as a *different* administrator account (not your own account elevated), files go to that account rather than to whoever is signed in to Windows.

**Projects you've already fixed by hand don't need anything more.**

The Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Drive connectors still need authorizing in your claude.ai connector settings, and the `backlog` MCP server didn't start. None of them were needed here.
